scenes.text: On November eighteenth, eighteen eighty three, some American cities heard noon twice.
Before that day, almost every town set its clocks by the sun.
Noon was simply when the sun was highest over that town.
Towns often signaled noon by dropping a ball or ringing a gong.
So when it was twelve twelve in New York, it was twelve twenty four in Boston.
And in Chicago, it was only eleven seventeen.
For railroads running trains between all those towns, that was chaos.
Back in eighteen seventy, Charles Dowd had proposed time zones one hour apart.
Later, William Allen developed the plan the railroads finally adopted.
At noon on November eighteenth, railroad clocks switched to the new standard.
In several cities the clock struck noon twice: once by old local time, then again by standard time.
In New York, the new noon came about four minutes earlier than the old one.
Not everyone loved it. One newspaper joked people would have to marry and die by railroad time.
Pittsburgh, Cleveland and Detroit refused to switch at first.
Congress only made the time zones official in nineteen eighteen, thirty five years later.
Would you rather live by sun time or clock time?

title: The day America had two noons 🕛
caption: On Nov 18, 1883, US railroads switched to standard time zones. Before that, towns set clocks by the sun, so some cities heard noon twice that day.
